name: Inverse square law
seoTitle: Inverse square law Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Inverse square law: work out final intensity (I₂) from the initial intensity and the initial distance. A free physics calculator with the formula, units…
summary: The Inverse square law calculator turns the initial intensity, the initial distance and the final distance into final intensity (I₂). Think of it as a shortcut for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Inverse square law calculator work?
sections.html:
The Inverse square law calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports final intensity (I₂) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the initial intensity (I₁), the initial distance (r₁) and the final distance (r₂).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Inverse square law calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Final intensity (I₂)=initial intensity (I₁) × (initial distance (r₁) ^ 2) ÷ (final distance (r₂) ^ 2)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Initial intensity (I₁) = 30 × 10⁰, Initial distance (r₁) = 30 m and Final distance (r₂) = 30 m. The calculator returns Final intensity (I₂) = 30 × 10⁰.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Final intensity (I₂) = 30 × 10⁰ should be roughly the size you expected from Initial intensity (I₁) = 30 × 10⁰ and Initial distance (r₁) = 30 m.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in times 10 to the 0, and convertible to any of the 69 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Scientific notation, opening in times 10 to the 0
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Scientific notation, opening in times 10 to the 0
  • Length, opening in meters

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Inverse square law calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the initial intensity, the initial distance and the final distance — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

faq.q: What does the Inverse square law calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns final intensity (I₂), derived from the initial intensity, the initial distance and the final distance. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Inverse square law calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the initial intensity, the initial distance and the final distance, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter initial intensity (I₁) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Initial intensity (I₁) opens in times 10 to the 0 and the chip beside it offers 69 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Final intensity (I₂) = 30 × 10⁰. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Inverse square law calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
